verses.text: You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.
The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.
You therefore must endure hardship, as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.
No soldier on duty entangles himself in the affairs of life, that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier.
Also, if anyone competes in athletics, he isn’t crowned unless he has competed by the rules.
The farmer who labors must be the first to get a share of the crops.
Consider what I say, and may the Lord give you understanding in all things.
Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, of the offspring  of David, according to my Good News,
in which I suffer hardship to the point of chains as a criminal. But God’s word isn’t chained.
Therefore I endure all things for the chosen ones’ sake, that they also may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.
This saying is trustworthy: “For if we died with him, we will also live with him.
If we endure, we will also reign with him. If we deny him, he also will deny us.
If we are faithless, he remains faithful. For he can’t deny himself.”
Remind them of these things, charging them in the sight of the Lord, that they don’t argue about words, to no profit, to the subverting of those who hear.
Give diligence to present yourself approved by God, a workman who doesn’t need to be ashamed, properly handling the Word of Truth.
But shun empty chatter, for it will go further in ungodliness,
and those words will consume like gangrene, of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus;
men who have erred concerning the truth, saying that the resurrection is already past, and overthrowing the faith of some.
However God’s firm foundation stands, having this seal, “The Lord knows those who are his,”  and, “Let every one who names the name of the Lord  depart from unrighteousness.”
Now in a large house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of clay. Some are for honor, and some for dishonor.
If anyone therefore purges himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, and suitable for the master’s use, prepared for every good work.
Flee from youthful lusts; but pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
But refuse foolish and ignorant questionings, knowing that they generate strife.
The Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be gentle towards all, able to teach, patient,
in gentleness correcting those who oppose him: perhaps God may give them repentance leading to a full knowledge of the truth,
and they may recover themselves out of the devil’s snare, having been taken captive by him to his will.

footnotes.content: Paul calls Timothy to be strengthened—not by his own effort, but by the grace already residing in Christ Jesus. The invitation is to stop leaning on your own reserves and lean instead into what the Lord has already placed there, waiting to hold you up.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The passing of faith from teacher to disciple—Paul to Timothy, Timothy to others—is not a chain of individuals but a chain of faithful hearts. Notice "among many witnesses": the whole congregation sees and knows this transfer. It's public, trusted, multiplied.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A good soldier expects hardship; it doesn't surprise him. Paul isn't asking Timothy to avoid suffering, but to walk through it as one who belongs to Christ and knows his Captain is already victorious. That changes everything about what hardship means.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A soldier on duty doesn't tangle himself in civilian life—not because those things are evil, but because divided attention costs lives. Paul is teaching focus: when you serve Christ, other good things must wait their season, or your primary calling suffers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The athlete who runs outside the rules doesn't deserve the crown, even if they cross the finish line first. Playing by the rules isn't a burden; it's the only way the victory means anything. Shortcuts aren't shortcuts—they're disqualifications.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The hardworking farmer earns his portion of what grows. There's dignity here: work your land, and the land feeds you first. Paul is saying the laborer is worthy of his wage—not by begging, but by the honest partnership of labor and harvest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul has laid down three images—soldier, athlete, farmer—and now asks Timothy to think them through. He's not handing Timothy answers, but inviting him into the work of understanding. Then he asks the Lord to give understanding in all things. We think, and the Lord grants wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead—this is the anchor. Paul calls Timothy back to the center when everything else is noise. The risen Jesus, of David's line, according to the Good News Paul preaches: this memory is Timothy's north star in every trial.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul sits in chains as a criminal—the world's judgment is harsh. But he makes a distinction that upends everything: the chains bind his body, not God's word. What they think they've imprisoned, they haven't. The gospel moves freely even when the messenger doesn't.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul endures all things—hardship, chains, shame—for the chosen ones' sake. He sees the people ahead, not the pain beside him. That's how love works: it fixes its eyes on the beloved, and what would crush a self-focused person becomes bearable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This saying is trustworthy—Paul marks it as something worth holding to. If we died with Christ in baptism, we now live with him. Our old self, buried and gone, has made room for his life to live through us. That's the covenant Timothy needs to remember.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Endurance brings reign—not ease, but partnership with Christ in his reign. But if we deny him, he will deny us. That's not cruelty; it's consequence. We choose what we cling to, and he honors that choice, though it breaks his heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If we are faithless, he remains faithful—and here is mercy breaking through judgment. When we stumble, Christ does not. He cannot deny himself; his nature is faithfulness itself. Our wavering doesn't change his character; it only shows us how much steadier he is.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Remind them of these things—the core truths, not endless arguments. Paul charges them before the Lord not to quarrel about words that lead nowhere. Some battles train the soul; word-battles only dull the mind. Know the difference.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Give diligence to present yourself approved by God—not by men or crowds, but by God. A workman who needs not be ashamed is one who has carefully handled the Word of Truth, treating it with the care a craftsman gives his tools. Your handling of Scripture shows your heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shun empty chatter—turn away from it actively. It sounds harmless, just words floating about, but it feeds ungodliness the way small breaches in a wall let the wind in. What begins as chatter ends as corruption of the soul.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Such words consume like gangrene—a physical disease eating living tissue. Hymenaeus and Philetus are named here: not in shame, but as warnings. Their false teaching about the resurrection already past is a sickness spreading through the congregation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They've erred concerning the truth, saying the resurrection is already past. When false doctrine takes root, it overthrowing faith—believers lose ground. Error doesn't just confuse; it destroys the footing people stand on to meet Christ.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God's firm foundation stands—while men argue and error spreads, this doesn't move. The Lord knows his own, and everyone who names his name must depart from unrighteousness. The foundation is both comfort and demand: you are known, and you are called to holiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In a large house there are vessels of gold and clay, for honor and dishonor. Paul is describing a home—a household—with many uses and ranks. Not all vessels are precious or displayed; some serve humble purposes. Yet all serve the master's house.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If anyone purges himself from these—from error, from falsehood, from ungodliness—he becomes a vessel for honor, sanctified, suitable for the master's use. It's not that God makes you useful; it's that your purging clears the way for his purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Flee from youthful lusts—not by white-knuckling, but by pursuing righteousness, faith, love, and peace alongside those of a pure heart. You don't overcome temptation alone; you run toward good companions and good desires that are stronger than the pull of lust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Refuse foolish and ignorant questionings—not because curiosity is wrong, but because some questions have no answer and only stir strife. A wise elder knows which battles aren't battles at all, just noise meant to pull you into the mud.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord's servant must not quarrel—a hard word for those who love to be right. Instead: be gentle toward all, able to teach, patient. These qualities aren't weakness; they're the strength of someone who has nothing to prove and everything to give.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In gentleness correct those who oppose you—correction wrapped in gentleness is an act of love, not judgment. And the goal isn't to win an argument, but to open the door for God to give repentance and a full knowledge of the truth. You can't force that door; you can only open it gently.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They may recover themselves out of the devil's snare, having been taken captive by him to his will. Readers today hear an echo in those enslaved by addictions, by ideologies that feel like freedom, by shame that whispers they are beyond recovery. Paul's confidence—that people can recover, that captivity is not forever—is still true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
